Here Ephraim mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor. Many Christians read the child Immanuel in 7:14 as pointing to Jesus (Matthew 1:23), while Jewish readers and many scholars see a child born in Ahaz's own time. The verse does not name Jesus; that reading is in the chapter's notes.

Here Israel mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor. Bible Atlas links Jesus because Christians read Immanuel (8:8-10) and the stone of stumbling (8:14) in light of the New Testament; the chapter itself does not name him.

Here Israel, Ephraim, Manasseh, Naphtali, Zebulun and Midian mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor. Many Christians read the child of 9:6 as Jesus, while Jewish readers usually take a king of David's line in Isaiah's own time. The verse does not name Jesus. The Arameans (Syria) and the Philistines are named in 9:12.
Here Israel and Midian mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor.

Here Ephraim and Moab mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor. The chapter names Edom, the land and its people (11:14), not Esau himself; Bible Atlas links Esau because Edom descends from him. Many Christians read the shoot from Jesse's stump (11:1) as Jesus; Jewish readers expect a future king of David's line. The chapter does not name Jesus. The Philistines are named in 11:14.
The Medes (13:17) and the Chaldeans (13:19) are named in this chapter.

Here Israel mean the people or land of that name, not the ancestor. The Hebrew in 14:12 is "shining one, son of dawn," said of the king of Babylon; "Lucifer" is the Latin Vulgate rendering. Many Christians also read the passage as about Satan, but the text does not name him. Assyria is named in 14:25.
